We already know, and will see again, that to deny this is to deny dialectic itself and the dialectical character of human existence.

For to accept the immortality of the “soul” is, by the same act, to give up freedom: to give up the revolutionary or historical character of existence, and therefore to deny that human existence is essentially temporal.
Second, human finitude necessarily implies that “gods,” whatever form they may take, do not exist. It therefore implies radical atheism.
This claim too is not immediately obvious, and only the Phenomenology itself will allow us to become convinced of it.
The reverse claim, however, is straightforward.

An immortal “soul” can exist after a person’s death only outside the natural world. Since this world is such that human beings within it are finite or mortal, a soul tied to this world and subject to its laws would also be mortal.
Not to be subject to those laws means to exist outside the world.
The existence of an immortal “soul” therefore presupposes some “place” outside the natural world and its space—that is, outside ordinary space.
But such a “supernatural” or “otherworldly” place would undoubtedly be “divine,” if the word has any meaning at all—or, if you prefer, it would be “God” himself, insofar as God exists.

On the other hand, if a human being is mortal—and especially if he can, in some circumstances, freely bring about his own death—then God’s “omnipotence,” and God’s power to subject the human being to himself, is thereby limited.
If the human being were immortal, there would be nowhere he could flee from a being more powerful than himself: “Where could I go from your presence, Lord?”
But if he can freely destroy his own existence, he can always escape the “divine” yoke.
God may rule him so long as he is something. But no one can rule over nothing, for the simple reason that nothing is not.
And if the human being can refuse submission to “God” and, in a certain sense, remove himself from God’s power, then such a “God” is no longer an authentic god for him.

In any case, if we accept that recognizing the existence of “God” means denying human freedom and historicity, and if we accept that recognizing human freedom and historicity requires us, conversely, to deny “God,” then we can say that recognizing dialectic necessarily entails radical atheism.
From everything said so far, we can also draw a conclusion already reached earlier: dialectic is anything but a method.
As we have just seen, dialectic is an entire philosophical theory, and in particular a theory of the human being.
And because this theory claims to be true, we must say that dialectic itself exists in reality, together with everything it contains, presupposes, and implies.

If we accept that the existence of dialectic is simply human existence—or at least that human existence is dialectical—then from the single fact that human existence is dialectical we can derive, as we have seen, a whole series of important positive claims.

For example, as we have just done, we can say that human existence, insofar as it is genuinely human—that is, insofar as it is essentially temporal—is necessarily historical, revolutionary, free, and atheistic.
Conversely, if we regard the human being as historical, free, and finite, we must also regard him as a dialectical entity.
And this means that all three fundamental dialectical categories—identity, negativity, and totality—are present in him.
Or, which amounts to the same thing, we must distinguish in him the dialectical “moments” of thesis, antithesis, and synthesis.
Let us therefore ask what, in the concrete human being, corresponds to these three dialectical “moments” and to the formal determinations described above.
To do so, we will once again make use of passages from Hegel himself—short and precise passages, this time from the Phenomenology (Chapter V, Part A, subsection c).
As a dialectical entity, the human being is always and necessarily synthetic.
Hegel makes this point at the beginning of the passage:
“The [human] individual is in himself and for himself.”
But every synthesis necessarily presupposes an antithesis and a thesis.
So after saying that the human being exists “in himself and for himself”—in other words, that he is synthetic—Hegel adds:

“But the individual is also in himself [that is, as thesis]; in other words, he also has a determinate original being (bestimmtes ursprüngliches Sein). […] This being, [that is,] this determinate body of individuality, is its originality (Ursprünglichkeit), its own ‘what-it-has-not-done’ (Nicht getan haben).”
The human being’s “existence in himself”—the human being as thesis—is therefore, first of all, his body, in the broad sense of the term.
In other words, to consider the human being as thesis, or under the aspect of thesis, is to consider him in the same way we would consider any animal.

And by “animal” here we must understand everything in him that is not specifically human—that is, as we will see, everything that does not depend on “negativity” or freedom and is therefore not historical.

This includes not only the body itself, in its physical, chemical, and biological aspects, but all its physiological and “psychic” functions as well: the whole of its “life” in the biological but not historical sense—that is, all of its life that is not sociopolitical.

And because the human body is inseparably connected to the entire natural world, to speak of the human being as thesis also means speaking about his connection with the world. It therefore means speaking about the world itself insofar as it is connected with the human animal as his natural “environment.”
The aspect of the thesis, then, is above all the natural aspect of human existence.
It is precisely what is not dialectical in the human being: what is governed exclusively by the category of identity.
Hegel emphasizes this in the passage.
When he says that the human being, considered as thesis, is a “determinate being,” he means that this being is determined in a “fixed” way: eternally and immutably.
It is therefore always equal to itself, always “identical”; in short, it never changes essentially.
Hegel calls it “original” because it is not synthetic. It is not the result of any dialectical process involving self-negation.
He could equally say that this being has not been “dialectically sublated” or “mediated.”
Put simply, a human being must also be a natural “thing”—in this case, an animal.
He cannot exist apart from his body or from the natural world to which that body belongs.
And this is easy to understand.

If, as we already know and will see again, everything genuinely human—or dialectical—in the human being rests on negativity, that is, on negation, then before a human being can negate himself he must first be something.
Only something can be negated; nothing cannot.
But since he becomes properly human only through this self-negation, before it occurs he must necessarily be non-human.
That means that he must be a natural “thing,” an animal.
For “negativity” is realized only through this specifically human self-negation. Before it occurs, only “identity” is realized.
Yet the human being as thesis is not merely an animal.
He can also be a thesis as a human being.
The human being is, of course, always synthetic. But we have seen that any synthesis can also be considered under the aspect of a thesis.
For this reason, a human being can be a thesis as a human being—that is, as something other than an animal.
We can say that the “body,” or the “human-animal”—the zoological species Homo sapiens—is the “original” thesis in the strict sense.
It was from this “animal” that the “first” human being originally emerged. And somehow, for reasons we do not know, from this still “animal” newborn there appeared a “human child.”
But the concrete human being with whom we are concerned is always already human in the full sense of the word.
He is not merely an animal, not merely a thesis, but also a synthesis.
So even when he functions as thesis, he does so as a human being.
The thesis that interests us, then, is nothing other than a synthesis that has long since become a thesis.
This is why we may call the being of the thesis “original,” but we must not take the word literally.
It is not absolutely or in itself original. It is original only relative to the particular human being concerned. It is what, in him and for him, comes first.

Hegel therefore speaks of the “originality of individuality”—that is, the originality of a human character which is necessarily synthetic, already a “result,” rather than an “origin” in the literal sense.
Hegel also explains what this relatively “original” element means.
It is what the person himself has not made.
In other words, it is everything “given” to him at birth and, more generally, everything he has “acquired” from others rather than created himself.
It is everything determined not by him, but by the “place” he occupies in the world—both the natural world and the historical, sociopolitical world.
What belongs to the thesis in a human being therefore includes not only his “innate character,” “talent,” “abilities,” and so on.

It also includes his “spiritual inheritance”: everything he has learned from other people, everything he has taken from them, everything that has happened in him, to him, and for him without his own active intervention.
A hereditary monarch, for example, belongs to the thesis insofar as his sociopolitical position is determined by birth, unlike the statesman who has “won” power for himself.
Everything that can be fully explained by a person’s membership in a social class also belongs to the thesis.
The slave belongs to it insofar as he was born a slave, has done nothing to free himself, and is entirely “satisfied” with what he is.
But the “master” belongs to it as well insofar as he has done nothing to “deserve” his status.
In short, everything that is simply present in a human being or in humanity without having been created by them belongs to the thesis.

Of course, insofar as humanity is genuinely human or historical, someone must once have “created” or “made” this existing state of affairs by negating some earlier one. In that sense, what now exists is itself synthetic.

But once it is no longer being made and has already been made—once it has become detached, so to speak, from the process that produced it—it is nothing more than a thesis, at least for those who merely “use” what has already been made or “enjoy” a nature independent of them.
And it is clear that the presence of such a human or historical thesis in human beings and humanity is just as necessary as the presence of a natural thesis.

For if a person’s existence is human only insofar as he negates what is “given” to him—and therefore negates himself insofar as he too is part of that “given”—and if human existence is human, that is, historical, only insofar as it involves revolutions, then all of this clearly presupposes the existence of something that can be negated.
And that negatable thing exists only insofar as it has not yet been negated: only insofar as it remains governed by the law of “identity.”
For the appearance of negation, or negativity, interrupts its existence.
Every revolution, in either the strict or the broad sense, necessarily presupposes some kind of old regime.
That “regime” was itself once created by the revolutionary negation of some earlier “old regime,” and so it is synthetic or historical.
But by the time a new revolution begins, the regime itself continues only “by inertia.”
People “use” it, but no one is actively “making” it anymore. Its “creative forces” have dried up.
It is simply “there,” devoting all its strength to preserving its “identity”—that is, to remaining equal to itself.
Such an “old regime,” in the broadest sense, is nothing other than a human or historical thesis.
And conversely, every human or historical thesis is nothing other than the “old regime” of a revolution that is beginning, or will begin.
Human beings and humanity, then, while dialectical—that is, while totalities or syntheses—are also theses.
But there can be no synthesis without antithesis, and no “totality” without “negativity,” which is the source or driving force of dialectic.
